title: Your own data
text: The published session description invited you to bring messy historical datasets. An hour is not enough to work on them together, but the sequence transfers. Here is how to start, in the order that worked for Imperial Careers.

title: Your own data
text:
Before you open a model

Pick one question and one small sample. Twenty records you can check by hand beat two thousand you cannot. Include at least one hard case.
Keep the source reachable. Every record needs a reference that gets a reader back to the page: volume, page, line or offset. If your text came from OCR, keep the page images available. You will need them.
Decide what a record is. A person? A posting? A mention? Imperial Careers has one person per resolved biography and one event per posting, and the difference between “entry instances” and “people” is the whole of step 4.
Decide what the output looks like. A map, a timeline, a network. Build it early, from the first sample. It is your error detector.

title: Your own data
text:
The sequence








Step
Ask the model to
You




Structure
Read the sample and propose fields, with two example records; write the prompt rules down
Decide what the question requires and what the source can support


Extract
Process the sample inside a script, keep printed wording, put inferences in separate fields, report failures
Audit every tenth record against the source; sort the findings into patterns


Clean
Cluster candidate duplicates and argue each case from a dossier
Set the merge rules; decide the hard cases; keep the reasons


Ground
Retrieve identities with a verifiable lookup, save the evidence and the date, gate on type and dates
Judge the links that matter; set the gate for the rest


Visualise
Build the view the question needs
Look for what is in the wrong place


Fix
Find other records with the same cause, change the rule, rerun, show what changed
Check the fix and the previously accepted cases that moved

title: Your own data
section: Rules that saved the project trouble
text:
Rules that saved the project trouble

Local identifiers first. Every record gets a stable local id before any external one. Add a Wikidata link only after retrieval and review support it. Nothing suitable? Keep the local id.
No identifiers from memory. A model will offer plausible Q-numbers. Treat any identifier that was not retrieved by a tool as unverified.
Ground to the historical entity, not the modern one. The Colony of Victoria, not the state; British Raj, not India. Where a surface means different places for different people, resolve per person, not per string.
Ties resolve to no merge. A missed link is recoverable. A false merge is not.
Model decisions and human decisions in different columns. Never overwrite one with the other. Export human decisions with a fingerprint of the data they were made on.
Fix the rule, not the record. Then look at everyone the rule touched.
Make the correction a test. The probe that found the defect goes into the test suite.
Report what the sample can support. Handpicked cases explain failure modes. A stratified sample measures precision for one stratum. Neither measures recall; for that you need the silver standard.

title: Your own data
section: Tools, and what they cost at scale
text:
Tools, and what they cost at scale
Two different jobs need two different kinds of model.

The agent that writes the pipeline reads your sample, proposes the structure, writes and tests the scripts, builds the review views and the atlas. This is hours of a frontier model’s time per project, in a coding agent. Imperial Careers used Claude in Claude Code.
The model inside the pipeline reads every entry and judges every cluster. At 100,000 entries the frontier models are too expensive. Imperial Careers used Qwen on shared university GPUs for structuring and for the never-biographied matching, with the frontier model’s in-session work as the reference set to measure it against.

The agent can write the pipeline so that the cheap model does the reading and the agent is only called back when something fails. Which operation produced a given record should remain visible in the output.
The presenter’s environment uses Claude Code as the coding agent and the WikidataMCP server for lookups. Any coding agent that can run code, read files and call a lookup tool will do. See Run it yourself.

title: Ground
text:
Every arc on the atlas needs a latitude and longitude for a place named in a Victorian reference book: the Colony of Victoria, the Central Provinces, British Guiana, a princely state. Modern gazetteers do not have them or mislocate them. Wikidata has an item for each, with coordinates or a link to the capital that has them. Once every place surface in the corpus was grounded to a Wikidata item, one query returned coordinates for all of them. Weeks of gazetteer work did not happen.
The second reason is composition. A historian of the Cape and a historian of Bombay who both ground to Q1800510 have joined their datasets without meeting. The longer argument is Jim’s; the short version is: ground to Wikidata, do not host your scholarship there.

title: Ground
section: Two ways to get a QID
text:
Two ways to get a QID
Retrieve it. The pipeline uses the WikidataMCP server’s vector search, which matches meaning rather than strings, then reads the item’s statements, then applies verification gates (type, dates, place) before accepting. Every accepted link has the retrieved evidence and the lookup date beside it. The Colonial Office List graph has 1,066 people grounded this way with a zero-false-positive gate, and 131,343 events grounded to a place.
Ask a chatbot. Paste the biography into a model with no tools and ask for the QID. It will give one. Sometimes it is right.

title: Ground
text:
Live: the lookup
The presenter runs the MCP search in the room. Suggested script:

Search “Henry Trimen botanist Ceylon Peradeniya”. Read the top hit’s statements: born 1843, died 1896, botanist. Compare with the entry: director from 1880, M.B., F.R.S. Supported.
Search “Ferdinando Hamlyn Price” with the career words. The top hit is Q123279571, “Ferdinando Hamblyn Price”, alias Hamlyn, born 1855, died 1942, described only in Tamil as a Sri Lankan politician, no career statements at all. The entry says mayor of Colombo three times. Supported, on the name, the dates and Colombo, and the pipeline’s gate had rejected it because the spelling differed.
Search “Elwood D’Arcy Tibbits Antigua”. Nothing plausible in the top fifty. Unresolved. Keep the local record and the search that was run.

title: Ground
text:
Live, or saved: the chatbot
Twenty long entries were chosen on 7 October 2026: twelve for people the pipeline grounded, eight it did not. Paste one into a chatbot with no tools: “Who is this? Give the Wikidata QID.” Then look the answer up. Score it: right, wrong item, invented identifier, or declined. The answer key has the pipeline’s QID and the MCP lookups.
What the lookups already show: of the eight the pipeline left ungrounded, three have a plausible item the vector search finds at once (Price, Henry Francis Wilson, T. J. Alldridge) and five have nothing in the top fifty. “Not grounded” means the gate did not accept; it never means “no such item”.
And the control. On 7 October Jim pasted the twenty entries into Gemini 3.8 Flash with no tools: “Parse these bios and ground the places, schools and people to Wikidata ids where possible.” The response is fluent and well organised, names every person and place correctly, and gives identifiers for everything. Scored against Wikidata:







Person identifiers given
16 (4 entries declined)


Correct
0


Resolve to something that is not a person (a plant, a patent, Thoth, an Iranian village, an archive series, a reptile)
6


Within a few thousand of the right number
7


Place, school and other-person identifiers given
142


Whose Wikidata label matches the name
43



The matches are the famous, low-numbered items: Paris, Canada, Singapore, Churchill. Nyasaland resolved to a disambiguation page, the Straits Settlements to a Danish triathlete, the Cape Colony to an Austrian goalkeeper, Joseph Chamberlain to a Swiss footballer. The model knew who; it did not know the number. A Q-number from memory is a string the model has seen near a name, and nothing in the response tells you which ones resolve.
The same day, the same twenty entries went to Claude Opus 5.5 in a chat with web search, told to report only identifiers it had seen on a page (response, scoring). Sixteen identifiers given, sixteen right, the same four declined. It found Prince, whom the vector search had missed, and it found that Gorges has two Wikidata items for one man. It also stopped at its tool limit before reaching a single place name; a second pass finished the schools and the other people and reached 17 of 138 places (CSV, 75 identifiers, all verified). Its first memory guess for George V was Q269, which is Tashkent; it caught that itself by reading the page.











Gemini, no tools
Pipeline: vector search + gates
Opus, with retrieval
Astra, with retrieval




Person identifiers correct

16 of 16 given

A third run, Astra medium with web retrieval, took 27 minutes and produced a structured file of 180 entities with offsets, confidence, a relation type, rejected candidates with reasons and dated evidence (scoring). All 155 identifiers resolve consistently. It grounded Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, the Union of South Africa and the rest to the period polities, and it recorded Penang Q188096, the item the pipeline had wrongly matched, as a modern proxy only. It is the dataset a historian would want, at about 80 seconds an entry, which over 27,526 people is 25 days of model time before the India Office List.
All three chatbots read the biographies correctly. The difference is where the number came from, and what it cost. And even the best column needs the historian: someone has to pick between the two Gorges items, and someone decided Harris was Harris when the printed birth year disagreed with the item.

title: Ground
text:
Three questions to keep separate

Does the identifier resolve to what was retrieved? A Q-number from a model’s memory is not a lookup.
Is that entity the one in this source? Name, type, dates, place, activity. A real item can be the wrong person. Price’s item has the right dates and no career; the match rests on a rare name and Colombo.
What does the link assert? That this entry is that man. Not every statement on the item. Not that “Ceylon” in 1880 is the modern state.

title: Ground
text:
Places are harder than people
The surface “Victoria” occurs in the corpus as the Australian colony, the capital of British Columbia, an electoral district, a gaol in Hong Kong, a district in the Cape, a county in Mauritius, and a town in the Seychelles. The grounding cache (rows) shows what that took: the bare surface grounded to the colony by default, context rules for officials whose other postings are in British Columbia, manual re-grounding for the Cape and Seychelles variants, and six surfaces deliberately left ungrounded because one QID would be wrong for someone.
You decide: supported, unresolved, or wrong, for each link that matters, and the gate that decides the rest. The cases the gate gets wrong are the subject of the next step.
Next: The map finds the errors.

title: Structure
text: A biography becomes one JSON object: name, birth year, education string, honours with award years, a list of career events, and how the career ended. Each event has a position, a place as printed, start and end years, an acting flag and a civil or military tag. The agent and the historian settled the schema on a sample of entries before any batch ran.

title: Structure
text: A biography becomes one JSON object: name, birth year, education string, honours with award years, a list of career events, and how the career ended. Each event has a position, a place as printed, start and end years, an acting flag and a civil or military tag. The agent and the historian settled the schema on a sample of entries before any batch ran.

title: Structure
text:
The prompt
The system prompt the pipeline sends with every entry (full text). The rules are the historian’s decisions, written down:

Extract ONLY what is printed; never invent or infer facts. events: one object per distinct posting. EXPLODE compound/concurrent clauses into separate events (e.g. ‘reg.-gen., 1887, and M.L.C., 1889’ = two events). place: the colony, territory, OR locality named in the clause, AS PRINTED. If the clause names no place, carry over the previous clause’s place and set place_inherited=true; do NOT guess or upgrade a locality to its parent colony. birth_year: only if explicitly printed (‘B. 1872’); else null. NEVER infer from the earliest career date. honours: decorations/orders with their AWARD year if printed in parentheses; these award-years are NOT career events.

Every one of those rules exists because an earlier run broke it.

text:
What came back
Trimen’s 1889 entry, structured (saved):

Plus education: "M.B. (Lond.)", two honours without years, no birth year, no terminal event. In the published graph the first and third events are placed (London Q84, Ceylon Q918153); “British Museum” is an institution, not a place, and stays unplaced.

title: Structure
text:
Two kinds of model
The reference set was structured in session by a frontier model acting as the coding agent: about 200 entries, each checked. The corpus was structured by Qwen on a shared university GPU inside the script the agent wrote, at a cost the frontier model could not match for 100,000 entries. The runbook for the loop is saved. Every record says which path produced it.

title: Structure
text:
The audit
Every tenth structured record was read against its source by a reviewer model and the findings were categorised (catalogue, reviewed pairs). Of the first 186 sampled:



Fully clean
129 (69%)


Records with a finding
56


Findings judged major
8 (about 3% of records)



Three of the findings, with the source beside the record (saved):
The ditto that was not resolved. Balmer’s last clause, “senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935”, came back with place: "do.". The rule says inherit; the model copied the abbreviation.
The appointment date that became a birth year. “BLAKELY, DONALD QUENTIN.—Clk., atty.-gen.’s off., B. Honduras, Apl., 1898.” came back with birth_year: 1898 and an event with no year. The prompt forbids exactly this. The same record expanded “off.” to “officer” instead of “office”.
The knighthood split in two. “KT. BACH. (1920)” came back as two honours, KT and BACH (1920). Three records in the sample did the same.

title: Structure
section: Why the fix was not a bigger model
text:
Why the fix was not a bigger model
The errors are not random. They are a handful of systematic patterns: a short list of abbreviations mis-expanded the same way every time (“off.”, “col.”, “govt.”, “offr. in ch.”), ditto marks left literal, one compound honour split, “mentioned in despatches” dropped. Each has a deterministic fix: an expansion table, a forward-fill pass, a merge rule, a sweep of the source for a phrase. The fixes run after the model and cost nothing per record. A frontier model on every entry would have cost more and would still have needed the audit.
You decide: what is an event. Whether an acting appointment is a posting. Whether “called to the bar, 1879” belongs in the career. Whether “leader of leg. coun. from 1906 to 1911” is a position or a description. The prompt records those decisions; the audit checks whether the model kept them.
Next: Clean: one person or two?

title: The atlas
text:
Fifty-six seconds. Every arc is one official moving from one colony, presidency or province to another, drawn from the career graph and played out by year, 1815 to 1966. The interactive atlas behind it lets you search a name, follow a career, and open the 186 people the pipeline found serving in both the Colonial and the India Office: Philip Edmond Wodehouse, Governor of British Guiana, then the Cape, then Bombay, is one of them, and a historian of the Cape and a historian of Bombay would each have known half of him.
What the atlas rests on, from the 4 September 2026 build:



Officials in the roster (both Lists)
46,926


Officials with at least one recorded move
16,287


Arcs drawn
36,431



Every arc lands where it does because a place name printed in a Victorian reference book was linked to a Wikidata item that carries coordinates, or links to the capital that does. Every arc belongs to one person because forty annual entries were resolved to one biography. Every arc has a year because a clause like “ag. comsnr., 1915-16; and from 1919” was read as two events, not one. Those are the three questions of the hour, and each was decided tens of thousands of times by a model and a few hundred times by a historian.

title: The atlas
text:
The loop
The project did not go OCR, extract, visualise, publish. It went round a loop, many times:

Build the pipeline with a coding agent: segment the biographies, structure them, resolve duplicates, ground the places.
Extract the whole corpus with a cheap model inside that pipeline.
Visualise the result in the form the research question needs.
See what is wrong. A premier of British Columbia sitting in Australia. South African postings landing at Harare. Two Baluchistans.
Fix the rule, not the record. The fix goes into the grounding cache or the resolver, with a test.
Rerun and re-emit, and look again at everyone the fix touched, not only the case you noticed.

The atlas is step 3 and step 4 at once. It was built to answer a question about imperial mobility; it turned out to be the project’s best error detector, because a wrong grounding is invisible in a table of 180,000 rows and obvious on a map. Step 6 walks through three of the errors it found.

title: The atlas
text:
Ten years ago
The same three problems at ten million pages: Trading Consequences (2012–2013) text-mined nineteenth-century commodity sources with the Edinburgh Geoparser, five institutions and a Digging into Data grant (Clifford, Alex, Coates, Klein and Watson, “Geoparsing history”, Historical Methods 49:3, 2016, doi:10.1080/01615440.2015.1116419).









Trading Consequences, 2013
Imperial Careers, 2026




Structuring
A six-stage pipeline adapted by computational linguists; a relation was “same sentence”
A schema and a prompt written with a coding agent in an afternoon; a Qwen model reads 100,000 entries inside the script


Grounding
GeoNames string matching; “Saharunpore” missed because the gazetteer knew “Saharanpur”; a bug put every “Italy” in a Texan town; F-scores 0.62 and 0.61
Semantic search over Wikidata with verification gates; “Victoria” six ways; a bug put the Union of South Africa at Harare


Review
Historians spotted false positives through the visualisations; false negatives were invisible
Same. The atlas found the errors; a sampled audit measured the rest



What changed is who writes the pipeline and how fast the loop from error to fix runs. What did not change is that the errors you can see get fixed, the errors you cannot see need a sample, and a corrected error should become a rule.
Next: The source.

title: Run it yourself
text:
The dataset
Everything here is drawn from Imperial Careers (data CC0, code MIT, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21079938). The finished graph is committed there as JSONL under data/kg/graph_stage3/ and data/iol/graph_stage3/; the README shows how to load it into LadybugDB or Neo4j in two commands. The pipeline code, the grounding caches and the method documents are in the same repository.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Rebuilding the exercise
python3 scripts/build_review_cases.py      # cases.json for the decision exercise
No network needed.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Running the grounding test
outputs/ground-test/bios.md has the twenty entries. For the chatbot column, paste them into any model without tools. For the retrieval column, use the WikidataMCP server (Streamable HTTP endpoint https://wd-mcp.wmcloud.org/mcp) from a coding agent, or its public search endpoint. Two things to know:

Use the vector search, not the string search. Wikidata’s ordinary search API matches labels by string similarity. The MCP server’s search_items uses semantic embeddings. It is rate limited; cache what you retrieve.
No identifiers from memory. Tell the agent, and check its output. Resolve every identifier you are given before you keep it; wbgetentities with a list of ids is enough to see what they are.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Running the structuring prompt
outputs/structure/extraction-prompt.txt is the system prompt. Send it with one entry as the user message to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and ask for JSON. The Imperial Careers repository’s col_match/kg/extract.py is the production version, with the validator that drops any place or year not present in the source.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Credentials
No file in this repository contains a credential, and none is needed for the exercises. If you configure an agent with an API key, keep it out of the repository.

title: Cleaning and Structuring Historical Data: A Working Session
text:
One dataset, start to finish
Two printed reference works, the Colonial Office List (1862–1966) and the India Office List (1886–1947), carry a terse biography for every senior official: born, schooled, every posting, every honour. The same man recurs in forty annual editions. The OCR garbles a name here and there. Two men who share a surname threaten to collapse into one career.
Over a few months, one historian with a coding agent turned those volumes into a knowledge graph and an animated atlas of imperial careers:




Colonial Office List
India Office List




People
27,526
19,400


Dated career events
180,470
124,694


Events located to a Wikidata place
131,343
80,238



The hour is about how, and about where in that process a historian has to decide something.

title: Cleaning and Structuring Historical Data: A Working Session
text:
Three questions
A historian turning a text into data asks three questions of it, and each has one decision only the historian can make. A model can do everything around that decision, at scale.

The model does

title: Cleaning and Structuring Historical Data: A Working Session
section: The second half of the method
text:
The second half of the method
Extraction is half of it. The other half is looking at the result in a form where errors are visible. The atlas was built to answer a research question, and it turned out to be the best error detector the project had. A British Columbia premier appearing in Australia, a cluster of South African postings landing at Harare, two nodes both called Baluchistan: each was seen on the map, traced to a rule, fixed in the pipeline, and re-emitted for everyone it affected. Build, extract, visualise, see, fix, rerun. That loop is what the hour demonstrates.

title: Cleaning and Structuring Historical Data: A Working Session
text:
Further
Worked answers, running it yourself, and the saved outputs in outputs/: the extraction prompt, the audit of a structured sample, the duplicate-resolution rules and a sample of clusters, the place-grounding cache rows behind the errors, and the project review that found them.

title: Worked answers
text: These are the preparer’s answers with the evidence, drawn from the Imperial Careers project’s own audits. Each decision is for the record in front of you.

title: Worked answers
section: R1 (Structure). Blakely’s record does not stand
text:
R1 (Structure). Blakely’s record does not stand
Reject. The entry prints no birth clause. Its only date, “Apl., 1898”, is the appointment, and it went into birth_year while the event lost its year. The prompt forbids exactly this inference. Also “off.” became “officer”. This record is one of eight major errors in the 186-record audit; the category is HALLUCINATION. The fix is a guard: a birth year may only come from a printed “B.” clause, and an event with no year while the entry has an unassigned date is flagged.

title: Worked answers
section: R2 (Structure). Balmer’s “do.” is not a place
text:
R2 (Structure). Balmer’s “do.” is not a place
Reject as it stands; accept once resolved. The clause names no place; the rule says inherit the previous one, which is the Kenya-Uganda-Tanganyika service. The model copied the abbreviation. Because this error is systematic across the sample, the fix is a deterministic forward-fill: any place equal to “do.” or “ditto” inherits the previous event’s place, with place_inherited set. No model rerun needed.

title: Worked answers
section: R3 (Clean). Abery and Carbery are one person
text:
R3 (Clean). Abery and Carbery are one person
Accept the merge. The rules allow a merge on an OCR surname variant when the forename and career are consistent and one identical dated event is shared. Here: same forename, same honour (M.B.C.M.), the same 1867 Ceylon appointment, and ABERY attested only in the 1897 edition where CARBERY also appears. The ledger records the reason: “ABERY is OCR garble of CARBERY”. A reviewer who wanted more could check the 1897 page image for the lost characters.

title: Worked answers
section: R4 (Clean). A’Beckett and Beckett are two people
text:
R4 (Clean). A’Beckett and Beckett are two people
Reject the merge. The cluster exists only because of the suffix key and the forename. Birth years are 62 years apart; the rule tolerates OCR noise of a digit, not six decades. The careers share nothing: Lincoln’s Inn and the Victorian bench against Nigerian telegraphs. This is the normal case in the cluster sample: the clustering is deliberately loose so that real variants meet, and most clusters resolve to “keep apart” in seconds.

title: Worked answers
section: R5 (Ground). “Union of S. Africa” is not Q5155572
text:
R5 (Ground). “Union of S. Africa” is not Q5155572
Reject. Q5155572 is the British South Africa Company’s territory, seated at Harare. Q193619, the Union of South Africa, is what the surface names. The error came from a containment match on the string “South Africa” during the manifest join; it affected 960 Colonial Office events and was visible on the atlas as a Rhodesia node with far too many arcs. The fix patched five cache rows with a stated reason, added a containment guard to the join, and left a note that pre-1910 “S. Africa” (about 100 events) is ambiguous between the Cape and the Union and needs a date-aware rule.

title: Worked answers
text:
R6 (Ground). Brewster’s “Victoria” is British Columbia
Reject the proposed grounding; ground to British Columbia for this person. Every other clause in the entry is British Columbia, and Victoria is its capital and an electoral district. A surface-keyed cache cannot know that; a per-person resolver can. The fix routed “Victoria” through a context rule (British Columbia signal in the career → Q1973, which geolocates to its seat; otherwise the Australian colony). Fixing it exposed a second bug: per-person overrides had never applied because the resolver and the graph keyed people differently. Both corpora were re-emitted.
What remains open: six “Victoria” surfaces (“Victoria district”, “Victoria county”, the Cape variants) mean different places for different people and are left ungrounded by design until each is resolved per person.

title: Worked answers
section: R7 (Ground, extra). Price is Q123279571, on the name and dates
text:
R7 (Ground, extra). Price is Q123279571, on the name and dates
Accept, with the evidence recorded. The item has a rare name with the alias covering the spelling, birth and death years consistent with the career (scholarship 1875, writership 1878), and a Tamil description meaning Sri Lankan politician, which fits three terms as mayor of Colombo. It has no career statements, so the match rests on name, dates and place of activity, and the record should say so. The pipeline’s zero-false-positive gate rejected it because the surname differs by one letter; that is the gate doing its job, and this is the kind of case a human review queue exists for. A reasonable person could also mark it unresolved pending a Ceylon directory; what they cannot do is treat the gate’s rejection as evidence that no item exists.

title: Worked answers
text:
The pattern
Across the seven cases the decisive evidence was never the model’s confidence and never the identifier’s existence. It was the source’s own words (“Apl., 1898” is an appointment; “do.” is a ditto), the dossier’s dates and careers, the item’s statements read rather than assumed, and the map. Every fix went into a rule, a cache row with a reason, or a test, and was then checked against everyone it touched.

text:
Mark it up yourself
Before the model does it, do it by hand. Open the mark-up exercise (or the paper handout in the room) and tag, in one entry, every position, place, year, honour, and the education and birth fields. Three minutes. Then press Compare to see what the pipeline extracted for the same entry.
Three things come up every time, and they are the structuring decisions of the next step:

Volumes OCR’d (Colonial Office List family, 1867–1966)

The India Office List is the same shape and was processed by the same scripts, rerooted to a second corpus: 19,400 people, 124,694 events.
We begin after OCR. The volumes were OCR’d with olmOCR on a Compute Canada cluster; other sessions cover that. What matters here is that OCR output is the input, with its garbles (“ABERY” for CARBERY, “ACARLTHUR” for McARTHUR), and that the page is one click away when a reading has to be checked.

title: The source
text:
Why this example

The entries are formulaic enough that a schema is obvious, and irregular enough that every tenth one breaks it.
The same person recurs across editions, so identity has to be resolved before anything can be counted.
The places are nineteenth-century polities, not modern cities, so grounding is a historical decision, not a lookup.
There is a payoff at the end that depends on all three being right.

Next: Structure.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
Trimen has an entry in seven editions. A long-serving official has one in forty. Across 85 volumes the Record of Services yields on the order of 100,000 entry instances that have to be resolved into 27,526 people. Most of that is easy: the same surname, the same given names, the same career a line longer each year. The rest is where the OCR has rewritten a surname, a man has changed his title, or two men share a name.
The design rule, stated before any code was written (approach):

A missed link is recoverable; a false merge silently corrupts the record. Every default resolves ties to no merge.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
Trimen has an entry in seven editions. A long-serving official has one in forty. Across 85 volumes the Record of Services yields on the order of 100,000 entry instances that have to be resolved into 27,526 people. Most of that is easy: the same surname, the same given names, the same career a line longer each year. The rest is where the OCR has rewritten a surname, a man has changed his title, or two men share a name.
The design rule, stated before any code was written (approach):

A missed link is recoverable; a false merge silently corrupts the record. Every default resolves ties to no merge.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
The passes

Deterministic passes merge on strong keys: identical name and birth year, identical name and a shared dated event, and so on. They did most of the work and were tested against 543 hand-verified careers with zero false merges.
Clustering the residue: biographies that share a spelled forename and the last four letters of the surname land together, so OCR variants of one person meet.
Adjudication of each cluster by a model reading a dossier: every version of every biography, with birth year, education, honours, the full dated career. The output is a partition into people with a reason for each merge, appended to a ledger (rules and loop, first 25 ledger entries). 917 groups so far.
A silver standard of 200 hand-labelled cases, built afterwards, to measure what the passes and the judge actually did. On the India Office List the deterministic tier scored 39 of 40 (one unsure).

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
The rules
Merge only on positive same-person evidence: an overlapping dated event, a near-identical education string, a shared honour with its year, or an OCR surname variant with a consistent career. Birth year is OCR-noisy and never splits on its own. Different spelled forenames keep people apart. And the decisive case: same name, adjacent birth years, divergent education or specialty is two people.

title: Clean: one person or two?
text:
Four clusters
From a sample of twelve, unedited:








Cluster

Both M.B.C.M.; both “1867 Ceylon Assistant colonial surgeon”; ABERY appears in one edition, CARBERY in six
Merge. ABERY is an OCR garble; one identical event suffices with the forename and honour


A’BECKETT, Thomas, b. 1836 / BECKETT, Thomas Rumbold, b. 1898
Suffix and forename match; a Victorian judge knighted 1909 and a Nigerian telegraph engineer of 1948
Keep apart. Birth years 62 years apart and disjoint careers


ABRAHAM, Henry Charles, b. 1887 / GRAHAM, Charles Drummond, b. 1901
Suffix “aham” and the forename Charles
Keep apart. Different first forenames, different colonies, no shared event


ABBOTT, Myles John, b. 1906 / IBBOTT, John Thomas
Suffix and a shared “John”
Keep apart. Hong Kong judge of the 1930s and a Demerara customs clerk of 1860



Three of four are easy once the dossier is in front of you, and that is the point: the model’s job was to assemble the dossier and make the argument. The ledger keeps the reason, so the next person can disagree with it.
You decide: the cases where the evidence is one shared event and a plausible OCR garble. Whether a peer’s family name and his title are one biography. Whether a “thin” fragment with a full given name and nothing else should join a career. Those went to a review queue ranked by how much the decision matters: career length, cross-colony span, seniority.
Next: Ground.

title: The map finds the errors
text: A wrong grounding is invisible in a table of 180,000 rows. On a map it is a dot in the wrong hemisphere. The project keeps a running list of defects surfaced while building the atlas, and a review of 3 September 2026 that re-fetched every QID in the graph and loaded the atlas headlessly to look for more. Three from those lists.

title: The map finds the errors
section: A premier of British Columbia in Australia
text:
A premier of British Columbia in Australia
Harlan Brewster’s 1918 entry (saved): newspaper work in New Brunswick and Boston, removed to British Columbia in 1897, elected for Alberni, “defeated by Sir Richard McBride, in Victoria, 1912”, re-elected at a by-election in 1916, premier of British Columbia 1916. The graph gives him two events as member for Victoria. The bare surface “Victoria” was grounded to the Australian colony, Q56850459, by the surface-keyed cache. The atlas showed a British Columbia premier with a seat in Melbourne.
Seen on the map. Cause: a cache keyed on the surface string, with “Victoria” resolved once for everyone. Fix: a per-person context resolver. If the official’s other postings signal British Columbia, “Victoria” is British Columbia (Q1973), which geolocates to its seat; otherwise the colony. Also found while fixing it: per-person overrides had never applied at all, because the resolver keyed people one way and the graph another. Repairing that fixed a second, unrelated split between the North-Western Provinces of India and of Ceylon. Both corpora re-emitted.

title: The map finds the errors
section: The Union of South Africa at Harare
text:
The Union of South Africa at Harare
Five surfaces, “Union of S. Africa”, “S. Africa”, “S.A.” and two more, had been joined to the Wikidata item for the British South Africa Company’s territory, Q5155572, because the join matched “South Africa” by containment. 960 Colonial Office events, 283 arcs in and 289 out, plotted at Harare.
Seen in the September review, on the map, as a node with far too many arcs for Rhodesia. Cause: a containment match in the manifest join. Fix: five cache rows patched to Q193619 Union of South Africa, a containment guard added to the join so it cannot recur, and the note that pre-1910 “S. Africa” is ambiguous and about 100 events still need a date-aware rule. The patched rows carry the reason (cache rows).

title: The map finds the errors
text:
Two Baluchistans
The colony layer had Baluchistan under Q843, which is Pakistan, for fifty India Office events, and a second Baluchistan node under a different QID. The atlas drew two nodes with the same label. Fix: one canonical entry in the colony table, the duplicate folded in. The same review found Penang grounded to the modern Malaysian state (1,083 events; label-locked so it looked right) and “Dutch East Indies” attracting “New Guinea” and “Australasia”.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
What a fix changes
Each fix is to a rule or a cache row, not to a record, so it applies to everyone the rule touched. After each one the pipeline re-emits both corpora and the atlas is rebuilt. The review then checks two things: the cases the fix was meant to repair, and the previously accepted cases that changed. The second group is where new errors hide.
The same discipline for structure: the every-tenth audit’s error catalogue became a post-processing pass with tests, and the three name probes that found the dedup defects are regression tests. The probe that found the error is the test that keeps it out.

title: The map finds the errors
text:
What the map cannot find
False negatives. An official whose “Victoria” was left ungrounded does not appear anywhere wrong; he simply has no arc. A merge that should have happened leaves two short careers instead of one long one, both plausible. For those the project built the silver standards: 200 hand-labelled cases, stratified so that the risky strata (rare surname, overlapping eras) are oversampled, scored against the machine output. On the Colonial Office List never-biographied population the judge’s “different” verdicts in the rare-surname stratum turned out to have a false-negative rate of 76 per cent, which no map would have shown.
Now: the exercise. Seven decisions, one reason each.
